q: Urine leaves the body from the bladder through the:
o: Ureter
Renal pelvis
Urethra
Collecting duct
x: The urethra carries urine from the bladder to the outside. Each ureter carries urine from a kidney down to the bladder.

q: Each kidney is enclosed in a tough, fibrous outer covering called the:
o: Bowman's capsule
Renal cortex
Renal capsule
Renal pelvis
x: The renal capsule is the protective fibrous coat around the whole kidney. Bowman's capsule is a tiny cup at the start of each nephron, and the cortex lies just inside the renal capsule.

q: The concave inner border of each bean-shaped kidney, where the hilum lies, faces:
o: Towards the front wall of the abdomen
Towards the vertebral column
Outwards, towards the side of the body
Downwards, towards the bladder
x: The kidneys lie on either side of the backbone with their concave borders facing inwards towards it. Renal vessels and the ureter enter or leave at the hilum on this side.

q: Each renal artery, which brings blood to a kidney, arises directly from the:
o: Inferior vena cava
Hepatic portal vein
Pulmonary artery
Abdominal (dorsal) aorta
x: The renal arteries are branches of the abdominal aorta, so the kidneys receive blood at high pressure. The renal veins drain into the inferior vena cava.

q: Urine leaving the collecting ducts at the tip (papilla) of a renal pyramid passes first into a:
o: Calyx (cup-like branch) of the renal pelvis
Bowman's capsule
Loop of Henle
Urethra
x: Collecting ducts open at the papilla of each pyramid into a calyx, a cup-like branch of the renal pelvis. From the pelvis urine flows down the ureter.

q: During urination (micturition), which events take place?
o: The bladder wall relaxes and the urethral sphincters contract
The ureters contract and the bladder wall relaxes
The smooth muscle of the bladder wall contracts and the urethral sphincters relax
The kidneys contract and push urine into the bladder
x: To empty the bladder its muscular wall contracts while the sphincters around the urethra open. When sphincters contract and the wall relaxes, urine is stored instead.

q: Young children cannot control urination, but older children and adults can. This voluntary control depends mainly on the:
o: Internal sphincter of smooth muscle at the bladder neck
Peristalsis of the ureters
External urethral sphincter of skeletal muscle
Valves at the ends of the collecting ducts
x: The external urethral sphincter is skeletal muscle under voluntary control, which a child learns to use. The internal sphincter is smooth muscle and works involuntarily.

q: Urine moves down the ureters to the bladder mainly by:
o: Gravity alone
Peristaltic contractions of the smooth muscle in their walls
The beating of cilia lining the ureters
Suction created by the bladder
x: Waves of smooth-muscle contraction (peristalsis) push urine along each ureter. That is why urine still reaches the bladder when a person is lying down.

q: A student compares the male and female urethra. Which of her notes is right?
o: In males it carries both urine and semen
It carries urine from each kidney to the bladder
In females it is longer than in males
It is lined by nephrons that reabsorb water
x: The male urethra runs through the penis and is shared by the urinary and reproductive systems. It is much longer than the female urethra; the ureters, not the urethra, link kidneys to bladder.

q: Bowman's capsule is best described as:
o: A tuft of capillaries lying between two arterioles
The fibrous covering of the whole kidney
The cup-shaped, double-walled blind end of a nephron around the glomerulus
The funnel at the upper end of the ureter
x: Bowman's capsule is the expanded, cup-like start of the nephron. Its two walls enclose a space that receives the filtrate; the capillary tuft inside it is the glomerulus.

q: Cells of the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle contain many mitochondria. This suits them for:
o: Absorbing water by osmosis
Filtering plasma out of the blood
Actively pumping sodium and chloride ions out of the filtrate
Secreting plasma proteins into the filtrate
x: The ascending limb pumps out salts by active transport, which needs much ATP from mitochondria. It is impermeable to water, and filtration happens only at the glomerulus.

q: The podocytes of Bowman's capsule help filtration because their foot-like processes:
o: Actively pump glucose into the capsule
Form a waterproof seal around the glomerulus
Leave narrow filtration slits through which the filtrate passes
Secrete hydrogen ions into the filtrate
x: Podocytes wrap the glomerular capillaries with interlocking foot processes. The narrow slits between them let water and small solutes through while holding back larger particles.

q: Fluid filtered out of the glomerular blood crosses which layers, in order, to reach the space inside Bowman's capsule?
o: Capillary endothelium → basement membrane → podocyte layer
Podocyte layer → basement membrane → capillary endothelium
Basement membrane → capillary endothelium → podocyte layer
Capillary endothelium → podocyte layer → basement membrane
x: Filtrate first passes through the pores of the capillary endothelium, then the basement membrane, and finally the slits between the podocytes of the inner capsule wall.

q: Compared with the cells of the proximal convoluted tubule, the cells of the distal convoluted tubule have:
o: A thicker brush border, as most reabsorption takes place there
Far fewer microvilli, as much less reabsorption takes place there
No mitochondria at all
Cilia that sweep the filtrate along
x: The PCT, where most reabsorption occurs, has a dense brush border of microvilli. DCT cells have few microvilli because they reabsorb a much smaller amount, under hormone control.

q: In the urinary system, urine is formed in the:
o: Nephrons of the kidneys
Urinary bladder
Ureters
Urethra
x: Urine is made by the nephrons of the kidneys. The ureters carry it, the bladder stores it and the urethra passes it out; none of these change it.

q: The urge to urinate arises when:
o: The kidneys stop filtering the blood
The ureters become blocked
The blood urea level rises above normal
Stretch receptors in the bladder wall are stimulated as it fills
x: As urine collects, the bladder wall stretches. Stretch receptors send impulses to the spinal cord and brain, producing the urge to urinate.

q: Going from the outside of a kidney inwards, which order of regions is met?
o: Cortex → renal capsule → medulla → renal pelvis
Renal capsule → medulla → cortex → renal pelvis
Renal capsule → cortex → medulla → renal pelvis
Renal capsule → renal pelvis → cortex → medulla
x: The fibrous capsule covers the outer cortex. Inside lies the medulla with its pyramids, which drain into the renal pelvis near the hilum.

q: The last part of the nephron itself, which joins a collecting duct, is the:
o: Proximal convoluted tubule
Distal convoluted tubule
Loop of Henle
Renal pelvis
x: The nephron runs Bowman's capsule, PCT, loop of Henle, then DCT. The DCT empties into a collecting duct, which is shared by several nephrons.

q: Which statement about the two types of nephron in the human kidney is correct?
o: Most are juxtamedullary nephrons with long loops
There are equal numbers of each type
Cortical nephrons have no loop of Henle at all
Most are cortical nephrons; only a minority are juxtamedullary
x: The large majority of human nephrons are cortical, with short loops; a smaller share are juxtamedullary, with long loops reaching deep into the medulla. Cortical nephrons still have a short loop.

q: Urinary tract infections are more common in women than in men mainly because:
o: Women have only one ureter
The female bladder has no sphincter
Women's kidneys produce less urine
The female urethra is much shorter, so bacteria reach the bladder more easily
x: Bacteria usually enter from outside through the urethra. A short urethra gives them a shorter route to the bladder, so infection is more common in women.

q: A beaver living in fresh water has kidneys with mostly short loops of Henle. This suits it because it:
o: Must make urine more concentrated than a desert rat's
Has plenty of water and does not need to make concentrated urine
Has no need to filter its blood
Loses water mainly through its lungs
x: Long loops build the medullary salt gradient needed for concentrated urine. An animal surrounded by fresh water has no need to save water, so short loops are enough.

q: The renal cortex looks granular because it contains:
o: The renal pyramids and long loops of Henle
The ureter and its branches
Large numbers of renal corpuscles and convoluted tubules
Only blood vessels and fat
x: All the glomeruli with their capsules, and the coiled PCTs and DCTs, lie in the cortex and give it a dotted look. The straight loops and collecting ducts make the medulla look striped.

q: A urea molecule filtered in a glomerulus is passed out of the body in urine. Which structure does it NOT pass through?
o: Renal vein
Loop of Henle
Collecting duct
Ureter
x: Filtered urea travels Bowman's capsule, PCT, loop of Henle, DCT, collecting duct, pelvis, ureter, bladder and urethra. The renal vein carries blood away from the kidney, not urine.

q: Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) means:
o: The volume of urine passed per day
The speed of blood flow in the renal artery
The amount of glucose reabsorbed per minute
The volume of filtrate formed by both kidneys per minute
x: GFR is the volume of filtrate formed each minute by all the glomeruli of both kidneys, about 120-125 mL per minute in a healthy adult. Urine volume is far smaller because most filtrate is reabsorbed.

q: Amino acids in the glomerular filtrate are normally:
o: Excreted in the urine as a waste
Reabsorbed only in the collecting duct under ADH
Converted into urea in the loop of Henle
Almost completely reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule
x: Amino acids, like glucose, are useful and are reabsorbed by active transport in the PCT, so healthy urine has almost none. ADH controls water, not amino acids.

q: In composition, glomerular filtrate is essentially:
o: Whole blood without its red blood cells
Blood plasma without its plasma proteins
Urine that has not yet lost its urea
Pure water carrying only urea
x: Filtrate contains water, glucose, amino acids, salts and urea at plasma concentrations, but blood cells and plasma proteins are too large to pass. Its composition is then changed along the tubule to make urine.

q: Which pair of substances both pass freely from the glomerulus into the filtrate?
o: Albumin and glucose
Red blood cells and urea
Fibrinogen and amino acids
Glucose and urea
x: Small molecules such as glucose and urea are filtered freely. Albumin and fibrinogen are plasma proteins and red cells are far too large, so each of the other pairs contains something that is held back.

q: Sodium ions are pumped out of the filtrate in the first coiled part of the nephron. Chloride ions there leave the filtrate mainly:
o: Passively, following the actively reabsorbed sodium ions
Not at all, so all the chloride ends up in urine
Only in the collecting duct, under ADH control
By being secreted back from the peritubular blood
x: Sodium ions are pumped out of the PCT filtrate, and negatively charged chloride ions follow them passively; water then follows by osmosis. Most filtered chloride is therefore reclaimed.

q: Which substance is NOT normally added to the tubular fluid by tubular secretion?
o: Hydrogen ions
Potassium ions
Certain drugs such as penicillin
Glucose
x: Hydrogen ions, potassium ions and some drugs are secreted from the blood into the tubule. Glucose moves the other way: it is filtered and then completely reabsorbed.

q: Filtrate forms at 120 mL per minute and urine at 1.2 mL per minute. What percentage of the filtrate is reabsorbed?
x: Reabsorbed volume is 120 - 1.2 = 118.8 mL per minute, and 118.8 / 120 = 0.99, so 99% is reabsorbed. 1% is the fraction left as urine, and 98.8 is the wrong result of subtracting without dividing.

q: In a person with liver disease, the level of plasma proteins is low. If other conditions stay the same, glomerular filtration would:
o: Decrease, because there is less protein to push fluid out
Increase, because the osmotic pressure opposing filtration is lower
Stop, because proteins are needed to carry water
Stay the same, because proteins are not filtered
x: Plasma proteins create an osmotic pressure that holds water in the glomerular blood and opposes filtration. With fewer proteins this opposing force falls, so net filtration pressure and filtration rise.

q: A kidney stone blocks a ureter, and pressure builds up in the tubules and Bowman's capsules of that kidney. Glomerular filtration in that kidney will:
o: Rise, because the capsule pressure helps push fluid in
Stay the same, because filtration depends only on blood pressure
Fall, because the back-pressure in the capsule opposes filtration
Rise, because more water is reabsorbed
x: Fluid pressure in Bowman's capsule pushes back against filtration. When urine cannot drain this pressure rises, the net filtration pressure falls and less filtrate forms.

q: The 'renal threshold' for glucose is:
o: The lowest blood glucose level at which filtration stops
The blood glucose level above which glucose begins to appear in urine
The amount of glucose secreted into the DCT
The blood glucose level at which insulin is released
x: The PCT carriers can reabsorb only a limited amount of glucose. Once blood glucose rises past the renal threshold, the filtered glucose exceeds this capacity and the excess spills into the urine.

q: Which statement correctly contrasts glomerular filtration with selective reabsorption?
o: Filtration is active and selective; reabsorption is entirely passive
Both are passive processes driven by blood pressure
Filtration takes place in the PCT, and reabsorption in Bowman's capsule
Filtration is passive and depends on molecule size; much reabsorption is active and selective
x: Filtration is driven by blood pressure and lets through everything small enough, useful or not. Reabsorption picks out useful substances, often by active transport using ATP.

q: Creatinine, a waste in urine, is removed from the blood by:
o: Reabsorption in the PCT only
Filtration followed by complete reabsorption
Filtration and also tubular secretion
The lungs rather than the kidneys
x: Creatinine is filtered at the glomerulus, and some extra is secreted into the tubule; little or none is reabsorbed. Complete reabsorption is the fate of glucose, not of a waste.

q: Although most solutes are reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule, the fluid leaving it is still isotonic to blood plasma. This is because:
o: No water is reabsorbed in this part
Water is reabsorbed in proportion with the solutes
Urea is secreted to replace the lost solutes
Plasma proteins enter the tubule there
x: In the PCT water follows the reabsorbed solutes by osmosis, so volume falls greatly but concentration stays the same as plasma. The fluid becomes hypertonic or hypotonic only in the loop of Henle and later.

q: Compared with plasma, what is the tonicity of the filtrate in Bowman's capsule, then at the tip of a long loop of Henle, then at the start of the DCT?
o: Isotonic → hypertonic → hypotonic
Isotonic → hypotonic → hypertonic
Hypertonic → isotonic → hypotonic
Hypotonic → hypertonic → isotonic
x: Filtrate starts isotonic. It loses water in the descending limb, so it is hypertonic at the hairpin, then loses salt without water in the ascending limb, so it enters the DCT hypotonic.

q: Tubular secretion takes place mainly in the:
o: Glomerulus and Bowman's capsule
Proximal and distal convoluted tubules
Ureter and bladder
Renal artery and renal vein
x: Tubule cells of the PCT and DCT, close to the peritubular capillaries, move substances such as H+ and K+ from the blood into the tubule. The glomerulus filters but does not secrete.

q: Which of the following is a normal component of healthy human urine?
o: Urea
Glucose
Plasma albumin
Red blood cells
x: Urea is the main nitrogenous waste in urine. Glucose is normally all reabsorbed, and albumin and red cells are not filtered, so their presence suggests disease.

q: The energy for active reabsorption by the cells of the proximal convoluted tubule is supplied as ATP by their:
o: Mitochondria
Ribosomes
Microvilli
Nuclei
x: PCT cells are packed with mitochondria that make ATP by aerobic respiration to power their pumps. Microvilli increase surface area but do not make energy.

q: The fluid that collects in the space of Bowman's capsule is called:
o: Urine
Glomerular filtrate
Lymph
Tissue fluid
x: Fluid forced out of the glomerulus into the capsule is glomerular filtrate. It becomes urine only after reabsorption and secretion along the tubule.

q: Tubular secretion usually needs energy because it:
o: Forces fluid out under blood pressure
Moves water by osmosis
Moves substances into the tubule against their concentration gradient
Moves only large plasma proteins
x: Secretion concentrates substances such as H+ in the tubule fluid, often against a gradient, so tubule cells use active transport. Filtration, by contrast, is powered by blood pressure.

q: Where along the nephron does reabsorption take place?
o: Along the whole tubule, from PCT to collecting duct, though mostly in the PCT
Only in the glomerulus
Only in the loop of Henle
Only in the collecting duct, under ADH
x: Every part of the tubule reabsorbs something: most solutes and water in the PCT, water and salts in the loop, and controlled amounts in the DCT and collecting duct. The glomerulus only filters.

q: Water reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule is called 'obligatory' because it:
o: Is controlled entirely by ADH
Takes place only when the person is dehydrated
Always follows the reabsorbed solutes, whatever the body's water needs
Requires ATP to pump water molecules
x: In the PCT water moves by osmosis after the solutes, whether or not the body is short of water. ADH-controlled water uptake happens later, in the DCT and collecting duct.

q: Because hydrogen ions are secreted into the kidney tubules, normal human urine is usually:
o: Slightly acidic
Strongly alkaline
Exactly neutral at all times
Strongly acidic, like gastric juice
x: Secretion of H+ removes acid from the blood, so urine is usually slightly acidic, around pH 6. Its pH varies with diet but it is never as acidic as gastric juice.

q: Which property of plasma proteins mainly keeps them out of the glomerular filtrate?
o: Their rapid active reabsorption from Bowman's capsule
Their secretion back into the blood by the PCT
Their large molecular size
Their attachment to red blood cells
x: Plasma proteins are too large to pass the filtration barrier, so they stay in the blood. Filtration works mainly by size, not by any later reabsorption or secretion.

q: Removing undigested food as faeces is called egestion, not excretion, because:
o: Faeces leave through the anus, not the urethra
Faeces contain no water
Excretion refers only to the removal of water
Most of the faeces was never part of the metabolism of body cells
x: Excretion removes waste products of the body's own metabolism, such as urea and carbon dioxide. Undigested food never entered the cells, so passing it out is egestion.

q: Urine that has a lower solute concentration than blood plasma is described as:
o: Hypertonic
Isotonic
Saturated
Hypotonic
x: Hypotonic means less concentrated than plasma; the kidneys make it when the body has excess water and ADH is low. Hypertonic urine is more concentrated and is made when water must be saved.

q: After several days of a very salty diet, aldosterone secretion falls. As a result the kidneys:
o: Reabsorb more sodium, so less salt is passed
Stop filtering sodium at the glomerulus
Secrete more water into the PCT
Reabsorb less sodium, so more salt is passed in the urine
x: Aldosterone makes the DCT and collecting duct reabsorb sodium. When it falls, more sodium stays in the tubule and is excreted, which restores the body's salt balance.

q: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus trigger more ADH release when they detect:
o: A fall in the solute concentration of the blood
A rise in body temperature
A rise in the solute concentration of the blood
A rise in blood glucose only
x: When blood becomes too concentrated, as when water is short, the osmoreceptors stimulate ADH release so that more water is kept. A diluted blood switches ADH release down.

q: The yellow colour of normal urine is due to the pigment:
o: Bilirubin
Haemoglobin
Urochrome
Melanin
x: Urochrome, derived from the breakdown of haemoglobin, gives urine its yellow colour. Bilirubin goes mainly into bile; its presence in urine suggests jaundice.

q: Besides the kidneys, which organ removes small amounts of urea, salts and water from the body?
o: Skin, through sweat
Lungs, through expired air
Pancreas, through its juice
Spleen, through the blood
x: Sweat contains water, salts and a little urea, so the skin plays a small excretory role. The lungs excrete carbon dioxide and water vapour but not urea.

q: Water reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct is called 'facultative' because it:
o: Always occurs at a fixed rate
Varies with the body's needs, under the control of ADH
Is driven by blood pressure
Takes place by active pumping of water
x: The amount of water taken back in these parts depends on how much ADH is present, so it changes with hydration. This adjustable step is the basis of osmoregulation.

q: Aldosterone increases blood volume because:
o: Water follows the extra sodium ions reabsorbed, by osmosis
It makes the glomerulus filter less protein
It pumps water directly into the blood
It stimulates red blood cell production
x: Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption in the DCT and collecting duct. Water follows the salt osmotically, so more water is kept in the blood and blood volume and pressure rise.

q: When blood pressure or blood volume falls, the kidneys release an enzyme that leads, through angiotensin, to aldosterone secretion. This enzyme is:
o: Renin
Rennin
Trypsin
Lysozyme
x: Renin from the kidney starts the formation of angiotensin, which stimulates the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone. Rennin, spelt with two n's, is the milk-curdling enzyme of the infant stomach.

q: A rise in the osmotic concentration of the blood causes more ADH release and also:
o: Increased sweating
A feeling of thirst, which leads to drinking
A larger volume of urine
Faster breathing
x: The hypothalamus, which senses blood concentration, also contains the thirst centre. Drinking adds water while ADH saves it, and both bring the concentration back to normal.

q: Besides keeping water and salt in balance, the kidneys help control blood pressure mainly by:
o: Adjusting blood volume through the amount of water and salt retained
Pumping blood back towards the heart
Constricting the aorta
Producing plasma proteins
x: Keeping back more salt and water raises blood volume and pressure; excreting more lowers them. This links the kidney's osmoregulatory work to blood pressure.

q: A diuretic is a substance that:
o: Decreases the volume of urine produced
Increases the volume of urine produced
Stops filtration in the glomerulus
Makes the urine more concentrated
x: 'Diuresis' means a large output of urine, so a diuretic increases urine volume. Alcohol and caffeine have this effect; ADH, an antidiuretic, does the opposite.

q: ADH is injected into a person who is already well hydrated. Which effect on the blood is expected?
o: Its water content falls and its osmotic concentration rises
No change, because ADH acts only on urine
Its water content rises and its osmotic concentration falls
Its glucose level rises sharply
x: ADH makes the collecting ducts reabsorb more water even though the body does not need it. That extra water dilutes the blood, lowering its osmotic concentration below normal.

q: A person with diabetes insipidus (no ADH) may pass many litres of urine a day, yet far less than the 180 litres of filtrate formed. Why?
o: The glomeruli stop filtering when ADH is absent
Aldosterone completely replaces ADH
Most water is reabsorbed in the PCT and loop of Henle whether or not ADH is present
The bladder reabsorbs most of the water
x: ADH controls only the final, facultative water uptake in the DCT and collecting duct. The large obligatory reabsorption in the PCT and loop continues, so most of the filtrate is still reclaimed.

q: The main component of normal urine is:
o: Water
Urea
Sodium chloride
Uric acid
x: Urine is mostly water, about 95%. Urea is the main dissolved waste, with salts and smaller amounts of uric acid and creatinine.

q: After a person drinks extra water, urine volume rises, but the total amount of urea excreted that day stays about the same. This shows that:
o: Urea is reabsorbed whenever water is drunk
The kidneys stop excreting urea when water is plentiful
Urea output depends only on how much water is drunk
Water output is adjusted separately from the removal of wastes
x: The kidneys change water output for osmoregulation while continuing to excrete the urea produced by metabolism. The two roles run side by side, one varying with intake and the other with waste production.

q: Keeping the osmotic concentration of the blood constant is important mainly because:
o: Body cells would otherwise gain or lose water by osmosis and swell or shrink
Enzymes in the blood need extra salt to work
Otherwise the heart would stop pumping
Otherwise urea would turn back into ammonia
x: If blood became too dilute, cells such as red cells would take in water and could burst; if too concentrated, they would lose water and shrink. Osmoregulation prevents both.

q: The control of ADH secretion, in which the effect of the hormone removes its own stimulus, is an example of:
o: Positive feedback
A reflex arc
Negative feedback
Countercurrent multiplication
x: A concentrated blood triggers ADH; ADH saves water and dilutes the blood, which then reduces ADH release. A response that cancels its own stimulus is negative feedback.

q: Urine tests can show whether an athlete has taken certain banned drugs. This works because the kidneys:
o: Store drugs permanently in the bladder
Make drugs from urea
Filter only drugs and no other substances
Excrete many drugs and their breakdown products in the urine
x: Removing foreign substances such as drugs and their products is part of the kidney's excretory role, so traces appear in urine and can be detected.

q: Even a person who is very short of water must still pass some urine every day because:
o: The bladder cannot hold urine for more than a day
ADH cannot be secreted during dehydration
Urea and other wastes can only be removed dissolved in some water
Filtration stops completely when water is short
x: The kidneys can concentrate urine only up to a limit, so excreting each day's urea needs a minimum volume of water. Here the excretory role sets a limit on how much water osmoregulation can save.

q: ADH travels from the posterior pituitary to its target cells in the kidney through the:
o: Nerves
Bloodstream
Ureter
Spinal cord
x: ADH is a hormone, so it is released into the blood and carried to the DCT and collecting duct cells. Nerves carry impulses, not hormones, to the kidney.

q: On a cold day with normal drinking and little sweating, a person passes more urine than on a hot day. This is because:
o: Cold weather stops ADH from being made at all
Less water is lost as sweat, so ADH secretion is lower
Cold makes the glomeruli filter less
More water is lost through sweating in the cold
x: With little water lost in sweat the blood stays dilute, so less ADH is released and the extra water leaves as urine. ADH is reduced, not stopped.

q: The kidneys are said to keep the 'internal environment' constant. The internal environment means the:
o: Contents of the alimentary canal
Fluid inside the urinary bladder
Blood plasma and tissue fluid that bathe the body's cells
Air inside the lungs
x: The internal environment is the fluid surrounding the cells: tissue fluid and plasma. The gut contents, bladder urine and lung air are effectively outside the body tissues.

q: Blood in the efferent arteriole leaving a glomerulus is:
o: Deoxygenated, having supplied oxygen to Bowman's capsule
Free of all dissolved solutes
Still oxygenated, since the glomerulus filters rather than supplying oxygen to tissues
Venous blood on its way to the renal vein
x: The glomerulus is a filter, not a site of tissue supply, so blood leaves it still oxygenated in an arteriole. It gives up its oxygen later, in the peritubular capillaries.

q: Blood flows slowly through the long vasa recta. This is useful because:
o: It does not wash away the high solute concentration of the medulla
It increases glomerular filtration
It allows plasma proteins to be filtered
It raises the blood pressure in the cortex
x: A fast flow would carry away the salt and urea that make the medulla hypertonic. Slow flow in the hairpin vasa recta preserves this gradient, so concentrated urine can still be made.

q: If the efferent arteriole of a nephron constricts, what happens to the hydrostatic pressure in the peritubular capillaries beyond it?
o: It rises, because more blood is forced into them
It stays the same, as the two beds are not connected
It becomes higher than in the glomerulus
It falls, because more resistance lies before them
x: Narrowing the efferent arteriole raises pressure upstream, in the glomerulus, but blood reaches the peritubular capillaries after passing more resistance, so their pressure falls further.

q: Which capillary bed lies inside Bowman's capsule?
o: Peritubular capillaries
Vasa recta
Hepatic sinusoids
Glomerular capillaries
x: The glomerulus is the knot of capillaries enclosed by Bowman's capsule. Peritubular capillaries and vasa recta lie outside, around the tubules.

q: If the efferent arteriole were as wide as the afferent arteriole, the most direct effect would be that:
o: Glomerular blood pressure and filtration would fall
Glomerular filtration would rise sharply
Plasma proteins would enter the filtrate
Pressure in the peritubular capillaries would fall to zero
x: The narrower outflow is what keeps glomerular pressure high. Without it blood would leave freely, glomerular pressure would drop, and less filtrate would form.

q: Water reabsorbed from the collecting ducts deep in the medulla is carried away into the circulation by the:
o: Vasa recta
Glomerular capillaries
Afferent arterioles
Ureters
x: The vasa recta are the peritubular capillaries of the medulla, running beside loops of Henle and collecting ducts. They take up the water and solutes reabsorbed there.

q: Kidney cells respire rapidly to power active transport. So, compared with arterial blood, blood leaving the kidney in the renal vein has:
o: More oxygen and less carbon dioxide
Less oxygen and more carbon dioxide
More glucose than it received
More plasma proteins than it received
x: Tubule cells take oxygen from the peritubular blood and add carbon dioxide from respiration. Glucose is reabsorbed back, not added, and plasma proteins are not made by the kidney.

q: Which statement about where the two capillary beds of a nephron lie is correct?
o: Both beds lie only in the medulla
Glomerular capillaries lie in the medulla; peritubular capillaries only in the cortex
Both beds lie in the renal pelvis
Glomerular capillaries lie only in the cortex; peritubular capillaries lie in the cortex and, as vasa recta, in the medulla
x: All glomeruli are in the cortex. Peritubular capillaries surround the convoluted tubules in the cortex, and their vasa recta branches dip into the medulla alongside the loops.

q: Which order shows hydrostatic blood pressure from highest to lowest?
o: Peritubular capillaries → glomerular capillaries → renal vein
Glomerular capillaries → peritubular capillaries → renal vein
Renal vein → glomerular capillaries → peritubular capillaries
Glomerular capillaries → renal vein → peritubular capillaries
x: Pressure is highest in the glomerulus, drops after the resistant efferent arteriole into the low-pressure peritubular capillaries, and is lowest in the veins draining the kidney.

q: The kidneys receive a very large blood flow for their small size. The main reason is that:
o: The kidneys store blood for emergencies
The kidneys make red blood cells
The kidneys need it to keep the body warm
A large volume of plasma must pass through the glomeruli to be filtered
x: The kidneys receive roughly a fifth to a quarter of the blood pumped by the heart. Such a flow lets them filter the whole plasma many times a day, far more than their own oxygen needs.

q: Blood enters each kidney through the:
o: Renal artery
Renal vein
Ureter
Hepatic portal vein
x: The renal artery brings blood in; it branches to supply the afferent arterioles of the glomeruli. The renal vein takes blood out, and the ureter carries urine.

q: If disease destroyed the peritubular capillaries but left the glomeruli working, which result is expected?
o: Filtration in the glomeruli would stop at once
Reabsorbed substances could not return to the blood, and the tubule cells would lack oxygen
Plasma proteins would start to be filtered
The urine would become more concentrated
x: Peritubular capillaries take up reabsorbed materials and supply tubule cells with oxygen and nutrients. Glomerular filtration depends on the afferent supply, so it could continue for a time.

q: Exchange of substances between the tubule cells and the peritubular capillaries takes place through the:
o: Space inside Bowman's capsule
Lymph vessels only
Walls of the ureter
Tissue (interstitial) fluid between them
x: Tubule cells move reabsorbed materials into the surrounding tissue fluid, from which they enter the capillaries; secreted substances take the reverse route.

q: Peritubular capillaries form a network wrapped closely around the tubules along their length. This arrangement suits them for:
o: Forcing fluid into the tubule under high pressure
Storing urine before it reaches the pelvis
Taking up reabsorbed substances and supplying substances for secretion all along the tubule
Filtering plasma proteins
x: Close contact along the whole tubule lets reabsorbed water and solutes enter the blood wherever they leave the tubule, and lets H+, K+ and drugs be delivered for secretion. Their pressure is low, so they do not filter.

q: Nearly all of the 180 litres of filtrate formed each day returns to the circulation through the:
o: Peritubular capillaries, including the vasa recta
Glomerular capillaries
Afferent arterioles
Lymph vessels of the ureter
x: Reabsorbed fluid enters the low-pressure peritubular capillaries and vasa recta, which drain into the renal vein. The glomerular capillaries only lose fluid.

q: Which pair correctly names one substance that leaves the glomerular capillaries in the filtrate and one that leaves the peritubular capillaries by secretion into the tubule?
o: Albumin; hydrogen ions
Glucose; hydrogen ions
Glucose; amino acids
Red blood cells; potassium ions
x: Glucose is freely filtered, and hydrogen ions are secreted from peritubular blood into the tubule. Albumin and red cells are not filtered, and amino acids are reabsorbed rather than secreted.

q: Which statement about blood leaving the glomerulus is correct?
o: All of its plasma has been filtered out
It has lost its plasma proteins into the filtrate
It has gained urea from the filtrate
Most of its plasma is still in it; only part has been filtered
x: Only a fraction, roughly a fifth, of the plasma entering a glomerulus is filtered. The rest, with the cells and proteins, flows on through the efferent arteriole.

q: Which feature is shared by both glomerular and peritubular capillaries?
o: Walls made of a single layer of endothelial cells
A supply from the afferent arteriole
A pressure high enough to force fluid out along their whole length
A position inside Bowman's capsule
x: Like all capillaries, both have walls one cell thick. Only the glomerulus is fed by the afferent arteriole, has high pressure throughout and lies inside the capsule.

q: The vasa recta are found mainly in the:
o: Renal cortex
Renal medulla
Renal pelvis
Ureter
x: The vasa recta are long, straight capillary loops that run down into the medulla beside the loops of Henle and back up again.

q: A drug bound to plasma proteins is hardly filtered at the glomerulus, yet it can still be excreted quickly in urine because it is:
o: Reabsorbed into the glomerular capillaries
Converted into urea in the PCT
Filtered together with the proteins
Secreted from peritubular blood into the tubule
x: What escapes filtration can still be removed by tubular secretion: the tubule cells take the drug from peritubular blood and pass it into the tubule fluid.

q: A person with liver disease has a low plasma protein level. In the peritubular capillaries this would:
o: Increase the uptake of reabsorbed fluid
Raise their hydrostatic pressure above that of the glomerulus
Have no effect, because proteins do not affect water movement
Reduce the osmotic pull that draws reabsorbed fluid into the blood
x: Fluid enters the peritubular capillaries mainly because their protein-rich plasma has a high osmotic pressure. With fewer proteins this pull is weaker, so uptake of reabsorbed fluid is reduced.

q: If blood passed through the peritubular network before reaching the glomerulus, what would most directly go wrong?
o: Glomerular pressure would be too low for effective filtration
The tubule cells would receive no blood
Plasma proteins would be filtered
The urine would contain red blood cells
x: Blood loses pressure as it crosses a capillary bed. Coming straight from the afferent arteriole is what keeps glomerular pressure high; after a capillary network it would be too low to filter well.

q: The medical term for the formation of stones in the kidney is:
o: Nephrolithiasis
Nephritis
Glomerulonephritis
Hydronephrosis
x: 'Nephro' means kidney and 'lith' means stone. Nephritis and glomerulonephritis are inflammation; hydronephrosis is swelling of the kidney from backed-up urine.

q: Within the kidney, stones are most often found in the:
o: Glomerulus, where blood is filtered
Renal pelvis and calyces, where urine collects
Renal artery, before blood enters
Bowman's capsule, around the glomerulus
x: Stones build up where urine collects and salts can crystallise, in the calyces and renal pelvis, and may then move into the ureter.

q: The sudden, severe, wave-like pain felt when a stone is passing down the ureter is called:
o: Angina
Heartburn
Sciatica
Renal colic
x: Renal colic is caused by the ureter contracting strongly against the stone. Angina is heart pain and heartburn comes from stomach acid.

q: Besides calcium oxalate, calcium-containing kidney stones can also be made of:
o: Calcium phosphate
Sodium bicarbonate
Potassium chloride
Magnesium sulphate
x: Calcium stones are of calcium oxalate or calcium phosphate. The other salts are soluble and do not form common kidney stones.

q: Which of these is a treatment for kidney stones rather than a cause of them?
o: Dehydration
A diet rich in oxalate
High uric acid in the blood
Lithotripsy
x: Lithotripsy breaks stones into pieces. Dehydration, high oxalate intake and high uric acid all raise the risk of stones.

q: Kidney stones differ from gallstones in that kidney stones:
o: Form in the urinary system and are mostly mineral salts
Form in the gall bladder and are mostly cholesterol
Form in the liver and are mostly bile pigments
Form in the blood and are mostly proteins
x: Kidney stones are crystals of salts such as calcium oxalate in the urinary tract. Cholesterol stones in the gall bladder are gallstones.

q: Calcium phosphate stones are more likely to form when the urine is:
o: Strongly acidic
Very dilute
Free of calcium
Alkaline
x: Calcium phosphate is less soluble in alkaline urine, so it crystallises more easily there. Dilute urine and absence of calcium would prevent it.

q: Taking very large doses of vitamin D for a long time can lead to kidney stones because it:
o: Makes kidney tubules secrete oxalate
Stops the liver from making urea
Lowers the water content of the urine directly
Increases calcium absorption from the gut, so more calcium reaches the urine
x: Vitamin D promotes calcium absorption. Too much raises blood and urine calcium, favouring calcium stones.

q: A patient confined to bed for many weeks after a fracture has a higher risk of calcium stones because:
o: Lying down stops glomerular filtration
Resting muscles release large amounts of uric acid
The kidneys stop reabsorbing water
Calcium is released from the unused bones and more appears in the urine
x: Bones that bear no weight lose calcium, so urine calcium rises and calcium stones form more easily.

q: A diet very high in common salt raises the risk of calcium stones mainly because:
o: Extra sodium excreted by the kidneys carries more calcium into the urine
Sodium chloride itself crystallises into stones
Salt makes the urine more dilute
Salt dissolves the lining of the ureter
x: When the kidneys excrete more sodium they also excrete more calcium, so urine calcium rises. Sodium chloride is very soluble and does not form stones.

q: Medicines that make the urine less acidic can slowly dissolve which type of kidney stone?
o: Uric acid stones
Calcium oxalate stones
Calcium phosphate stones
Struvite stones
x: Uric acid is much more soluble in less acidic urine, so these stones can dissolve. Calcium phosphate and struvite stones actually form more easily in alkaline urine.

q: Which treatment removes a kidney stone with no cut in the skin, using a thin telescope passed up through the urethra and bladder?
o: Open surgery
Ureteroscopy
Keyhole surgery through the back
Kidney transplant
x: In ureteroscopy the instrument goes up the natural urinary passages to reach the stone. Keyhole and open surgery both need a cut.

q: Laser treatment of a kidney stone works by:
o: Dissolving the stone with strong acid
Freezing the stone so that it shrinks
Drawing the stone out through the skin
Breaking the stone into small fragments with focused light energy
x: A laser fibre brought up to the stone delivers intense light energy that shatters it, and the fragments pass out or are removed.

q: Which pair correctly matches a kidney stone treatment with how it works?
o: Keyhole surgery: the stone is dissolved by drugs
Shock-wave lithotripsy: waves from outside the body break the stone
Ureteroscopy: the stone is removed through a cut in the abdomen
Open surgery: the stone is broken by waves through intact skin
x: Shock-wave lithotripsy breaks the stone from outside. Keyhole surgery uses a small cut, ureteroscopy uses no cut, and open surgery uses a large cut.

q: A cook works long hours in a hot kitchen, drinks little water and passes small amounts of dark urine. Which advice lowers his risk of kidney stones?
o: Eat more meat and salt
Drink enough water to pass plenty of pale urine
Take extra vitamin D tablets
Drink as little as possible to rest the kidneys
x: Plenty of water keeps urine dilute so salts stay dissolved. Extra meat, salt and vitamin D all raise stone risk.

q: Some cancer treatments kill very large numbers of cells at once. This can cause uric acid stones because:
o: Dead cells release oxalate into the blood
The drugs raise blood calcium directly
Nucleic acids from the dead cells are broken down, releasing purines that form uric acid
Dead cells block the glomeruli
x: In humans purines from nucleic acids are broken down to uric acid. Massive cell death floods the blood and urine with uric acid, which can crystallise.

q: A patient with a stone stuck in the ureter develops fever and chills. This most likely means that:
o: The stone has dissolved completely
Urine trapped above the stone has become infected
The kidney is making extra urine
The stone has passed into the bladder
x: Urine that cannot drain becomes a site for bacterial growth, and the infection causes fever. A passed or dissolved stone would relieve the problem.

q: Many people who have had one kidney stone form another later. The main reason is that:
o: Stone fragments regrow inside the bloodstream
The conditions that caused the first stone, such as low fluid intake, often continue
Lithotripsy makes the kidneys produce stones
Kidney stones are passed between people by infection
x: Unless the cause, such as concentrated urine or high urinary calcium, is corrected, new crystals keep forming. Stones are not infectious and do not grow in blood.

q: Which is the correct order of steps in shock-wave lithotripsy?
o: Waves focused on stone, stone located, fragments pass in urine, stone breaks up
Fragments pass in urine, stone located, waves focused, stone breaks up
Stone located by imaging, waves focused on it, stone breaks up, fragments pass in urine
Stone breaks up, stone located, waves focused, fragments pass in urine
x: The stone must first be located so the waves can be aimed at it; only after it breaks can the small pieces be passed in the urine.

q: Urine is said to be supersaturated with calcium oxalate when:
o: The urine contains no calcium oxalate at all
All the calcium oxalate is already solid
The urine is more dilute than blood plasma
More calcium oxalate is dissolved than the urine can normally hold, so crystals can form
x: Supersaturation means the salt concentration is above its normal solubility limit, which is the condition that allows crystals and stones to form.

q: P and Q excrete equal amounts of uric acid daily. P passes 1 litre of urine at pH 5; Q passes 2 litres at pH 6.5. Who is at greater risk of uric acid stones, and why?
o: P, because the urine is more concentrated and more acidic
Q, because the urine volume is larger
Q, because the urine is less acidic
Both equally, because the amount of uric acid is the same
x: Uric acid crystallises when urine is concentrated and acidic. P's urine is twice as concentrated and more acidic, so P has the higher risk.

q: A person whose blood calcium is normal is told she has formed a kidney stone. Which explanation is correct?
o: Stones can form with normal blood calcium if the urine is very concentrated
Stones form only when blood calcium is above normal
Stones form only in people who have gout
Stones form only inside the urinary bladder
x: Stone formation depends on the concentration of salts in urine, so low urine volume alone can cause it. Gout and high blood calcium are risk factors, not requirements.

q: Which combination of habits gives the greatest risk of calcium oxalate stones?
o: High fluid intake, low-oxalate diet, low-salt diet
High fluid intake, high-oxalate diet, low-salt diet
Low fluid intake, low-oxalate diet, low-salt diet
Low fluid intake, high-oxalate diet, high-salt diet
x: Concentrated urine, extra oxalate and extra calcium excretion from high salt all push calcium oxalate towards crystallising.

q: A build-up of urea and other nitrogenous wastes in the blood because of kidney failure is called:
o: Anaemia
Glycosuria
Jaundice
Uraemia
x: Uraemia means 'urine in the blood': wastes the kidneys should remove stay in the plasma. Glycosuria is glucose in urine; jaundice is due to bile pigments.

q: A person with normal fluid intake starts passing very little urine each day. This suggests:
o: Diabetes insipidus
Drinking too much water
Kidney failure
Overactive sweat glands only
x: A sharp fall in urine output (oliguria) is a typical sign that the kidneys are failing. Diabetes insipidus causes large volumes of dilute urine.

q: Severe dehydration from cholera or prolonged diarrhoea can cause acute kidney failure because:
o: Blood volume falls, so too little blood reaches the kidneys to be filtered
Cholera bacteria grow inside the nephrons
Diarrhoea fluid flows back into the ureters
The kidneys reabsorb too much glucose
x: Heavy fluid loss lowers blood volume and pressure, so filtration in the glomeruli falls and the kidney tissue is starved of blood.

q: An elderly man with a greatly enlarged prostate gland develops kidney failure. The likely reason is that the prostate:
o: Secretes urea into the blood
Destroys red blood cells in the kidney
Blocks urine outflow, so pressure builds back up into the kidneys
Stops the glomeruli from receiving blood
x: The prostate surrounds the urethra. If it obstructs urine flow, urine backs up and the rising pressure damages the kidneys.

q: A transfusion of the wrong blood group can damage the kidneys because:
o: Destroyed red cells release haemoglobin, which can block and damage the kidney tubules
Antibodies in the donor blood dissolve the glomeruli
The donor blood contains extra urea
The donor plasma stops urine from forming in the bladder
x: In a mismatched transfusion the red cells burst; the released haemoglobin is filtered and can clog and injure the tubules, causing acute kidney failure.

q: Taking large amounts of certain painkillers regularly for years can lead to chronic kidney failure because these drugs:
o: Make the bladder muscle contract permanently
Are converted into uric acid stones
Stop the liver from producing urea
Can slowly damage the kidney tissue
x: Long-term overuse of some painkillers gradually injures kidney tissue, a recognised cause of chronic kidney failure.

q: Repeated untreated bacterial infections that spread up from the bladder into the kidneys can lead to:
o: Scarring of the kidneys and eventually kidney failure
Stones made of sodium chloride
An increase in the number of nephrons
Larger, more efficient kidneys
x: Infection of kidney tissue causes inflammation and scarring. Scarred nephrons stop working, and repeated damage can end in kidney failure.

q: In kidney failure, a high level of potassium in the blood is dangerous mainly because it can:
o: Cause stones in the gall bladder
Increase red blood cell production
Make the urine strongly alkaline
Disturb the rhythm of the heart
x: Healthy kidneys excrete excess potassium. When it builds up, it upsets the electrical activity of heart muscle and can cause dangerous rhythms.

q: Many patients with chronic kidney failure become anaemic. This is mainly because the damaged kidneys:
o: Make less erythropoietin, the hormone that stimulates red blood cell production
Filter red blood cells out into the urine
Produce too much urea, which bursts red cells
Store iron instead of releasing it
x: The kidneys release erythropoietin, which stimulates the bone marrow to make red cells. Less of it means fewer red cells. Healthy or damaged glomeruli do not normally filter whole cells.

q: High blood pressure can be a result of kidney failure, not only a cause. It results because failing kidneys:
o: Make too much urea
Retain salt and water, so blood volume increases
Remove too much water from the blood
Release all their nephrons into the blood
x: When the kidneys cannot excrete enough salt and water, the extra fluid raises blood volume and therefore blood pressure.

q: A patient with kidney failure is often advised to limit dietary protein because:
o: Protein turns into glucose in the urine
Breakdown of excess protein produces urea, which the kidneys cannot remove well
Protein blocks the dialysis membrane
Protein makes the blood clot
x: Excess amino acids are deaminated and their nitrogen is turned into urea. Less protein means less urea for the failing kidneys to clear.

q: Why is a patient with severe kidney failure often told to drink only limited amounts of fluid?
o: Water damages the dialysis machine
Water raises blood glucose
The kidneys cannot remove the extra water, so it builds up in the body
Extra water produces more urea
x: Without working kidneys, excess water is not excreted; it accumulates, causing swelling, high blood pressure and even fluid in the lungs.

q: A fall in a person's glomerular filtration rate (GFR) means that:
o: More urine is being produced each minute
The kidneys are reabsorbing more glucose
Glomerular blood pressure has risen
Less plasma is being filtered by the kidneys each minute
x: GFR is the volume of plasma filtered per minute. A falling GFR is the key sign that kidney function is declining; a rise in glomerular pressure would increase it.

q: A patient whose kidneys work at only a small fraction of normal (end-stage kidney failure) needs, to survive:
o: Regular dialysis or a kidney transplant
Only a course of antibiotics
Shock-wave lithotripsy
A high-protein diet
x: At end stage the kidneys can no longer keep the blood clean, so either dialysis or a transplanted kidney must take over their work.

q: A healthy adult can safely donate one kidney to a relative because:
o: The donated kidney grows back within months
The liver takes over the work of the kidney
One healthy kidney can do enough work to keep the body healthy
Each kidney works for only half the day
x: The kidneys have a large spare capacity, so one healthy kidney is enough for normal life. A removed kidney does not regrow.

q: In peritoneal dialysis the fluid contains a high concentration of glucose. This helps to:
o: Feed the cells of the peritoneum
Draw excess water out of the blood by osmosis
Prevent the blood from clotting
Kill bacteria in the abdomen
x: The glucose makes the fluid hypertonic to the blood, so water moves out of the blood across the peritoneum by osmosis, removing the extra water that the kidneys cannot.

q: A known risk of peritoneal dialysis is:
o: Rejection of the fluid by the immune system
Formation of kidney stones in the catheter
Infection of the lining of the abdominal cavity (peritonitis)
Loss of red blood cells into the fluid
x: Fluid is put into the abdomen through a catheter, so bacteria can enter and infect the peritoneum. Cells cannot cross the membrane.

q: For long-term haemodialysis, a surgeon often joins an artery to a vein in the patient's arm. This is done to:
o: Lower the blood pressure permanently
Increase the volume of urine
Prevent rejection of the machine
Make a large, strong blood vessel that can be used again and again
x: Joining an artery to a vein (a fistula) enlarges the vein so needles can be inserted repeatedly and blood can flow fast enough to and from the machine.

q: People with chronic kidney failure often develop weak bones. One reason is that healthy kidneys normally:
o: Make calcium from urea
Convert vitamin D into its active form, which helps absorb calcium
Produce parathyroid hormone
Store phosphate inside the medulla
x: Active vitamin D is needed to absorb calcium from the gut. Damaged kidneys make less of it, so bones lose calcium. Parathyroid hormone comes from the parathyroid glands.

q: In a kidney transplant, the ureter of the donor kidney is joined to the patient's:
o: Urinary bladder
Liver
Large intestine
Urethra directly at the penis
x: The new kidney's ureter drains urine into the bladder, just as a natural ureter does.

q: Which of these patients is most likely to develop chronic, rather than acute, kidney failure?
o: A woman who lost much blood in childbirth
A child severely dehydrated by diarrhoea
A man given a mismatched blood transfusion
A man with poorly controlled diabetes for 20 years
x: Long-standing diabetes damages the glomeruli slowly over years, giving chronic failure. Blood loss, dehydration and mismatched transfusion cause sudden, acute failure.

q: Which measure helps prevent chronic kidney failure in a person with diabetes?
o: Eating extra salt every day
Keeping blood glucose and blood pressure well controlled
Drinking as little water as possible
Taking painkillers daily
x: Diabetes and high blood pressure are the main causes of chronic kidney failure, so controlling both protects the glomeruli.

q: Which set of blood results fits untreated kidney failure?
o: Low urea, low potassium, more alkaline blood
Raised urea, raised potassium, more acidic blood
Raised urea, low potassium, more alkaline blood
Low urea, raised potassium, normal pH
x: Failing kidneys cannot excrete urea, potassium or hydrogen ions, so all three build up: urea and potassium rise and the blood becomes more acidic.

q: Animals whose body temperature changes with the temperature of their surroundings are called:
o: Homeotherms
Endotherms
Poikilotherms
Heterotrophs
x: Poikilotherms have a variable body temperature; homeotherms keep it constant. Heterotroph refers to nutrition, not temperature.

q: A dangerous fall of core body temperature below normal, for example after long exposure to cold, is called:
o: Hyperthermia
Fever
Hibernation
Hypothermia
x: Hypo means below. Hyperthermia and fever are rises in temperature; hibernation is a controlled state in some animals.

q: A person sitting on a cold stone bench loses heat to it mainly by:
o: Radiation
Evaporation
Convection
Conduction
x: Conduction is heat transfer by direct contact between the body and a colder solid surface.

q: A person standing in a cold wind loses heat faster than in still air at the same temperature, mainly by:
o: Conduction
Convection
Radiation
Evaporation
x: Moving air keeps replacing the warmed layer of air next to the skin, so heat is carried away faster by convection.

q: On a sunny winter day a person feels warm standing in sunlight although the air is cold. The heat reaches the body mainly by:
o: Conduction
Convection
Radiation
Evaporation
x: Sunlight transfers heat as radiation, which needs no contact and does not depend on warming the air.

q: Heatstroke occurs when:
o: The hypothalamic set point falls below normal
The body's cooling fails and core temperature rises to a dangerous level
Shivering raises the body temperature slightly
Skin arterioles constrict in cold air
x: In heatstroke, heat gain exceeds heat loss and sweating may fail, so core temperature climbs high enough to damage proteins and the brain.

q: The part of the hypothalamus that starts sweating and dilation of skin arterioles when the blood becomes too warm is the:
o: Heat-gain centre
Respiratory centre
Heat-loss centre
Thirst centre
x: The heat-loss centre triggers cooling responses; the heat-gain centre triggers shivering and vasoconstriction.

q: If the heat-gain centre of the hypothalamus were damaged, which responses in a cold room would most likely fail?
o: Sweating and panting
Shivering and constriction of skin arterioles
Dilation of skin arterioles
Increased sweating only
x: The heat-gain centre drives the warming responses: shivering and vasoconstriction. Sweating and vasodilation are cooling responses run by the heat-loss centre.

q: Whales and seals living in icy water keep warm mainly because they have:
o: A thick layer of fat (blubber) under the skin that insulates the body
Many active sweat glands
Widely dilated skin arterioles
A large surface area to volume ratio
x: Blubber is a poor conductor of heat, so it greatly reduces heat loss to the cold water. A large surface area to volume ratio would increase heat loss.

q: The desert fox has very large ears while the Arctic fox has small ears. Large ears suit the desert fox because they:
o: Trap air to insulate the head
Give a large surface area for losing heat
Store fat for the winter
Reduce blood flow to the skin
x: Thin ears with many blood vessels act as radiators. In the cold, small ears reduce heat loss.

q: 'Goose bumps' appear on human skin in the cold because:
o: Sweat glands swell up
Skin arterioles dilate
Tiny muscles attached to the hair follicles contract
Fat cells under the skin divide
x: Contraction of the hair erector muscles pulls the hairs upright and raises small bumps; in humans this gives little insulation.

q: In a hot environment, the hypothalamus switches on the sweat glands by means of:
o: Thyroxine in the blood
Insulin in the blood
Lymph flowing to the skin
Nerve impulses
x: Sweating is a fast response controlled by nerves from the hypothalamus. Thyroxine acts slowly on metabolic rate.

q: Snakes and lizards are slow and sluggish on cold mornings because:
o: Their low body temperature slows their enzyme-controlled metabolism
They have used up all their stored fat
Their hypothalamus switches off at night
Their blood freezes overnight
x: Ectotherms take up the temperature of their surroundings, and at low temperature their enzymes work slowly, so muscle activity is slow.

q: A major advantage of being an endotherm is that the animal:
o: Can remain active in cold conditions when ectotherms are sluggish
Needs less food than an ectotherm of the same size
Does not need a hypothalamus
Never loses heat to the surroundings
x: A steady, warm body temperature keeps enzymes working at a high rate whatever the weather. The cost is that endotherms need more food.

q: Hibernation helps some mammals survive winter because:
o: Raising body temperature prevents them from freezing
Lowering body temperature and metabolic rate saves stored energy when food is scarce
They feed continuously during hibernation
They permanently become ectotherms
x: In hibernation the set point is lowered so far less energy is spent keeping warm, letting stored fat last through the winter.

q: In sudden cold, the adrenal glands release adrenaline, which helps raise body heat by:
o: Activating the sweat glands
Dilating the skin arterioles
Increasing the rate of metabolism
Slowing the heart rate
x: Adrenaline speeds up metabolism for a short time, releasing extra heat. Thyroxine has a similar but longer-term effect.

q: The heat that keeps a resting human warm comes mainly from:
o: Metabolic reactions such as respiration in the liver and muscles
Heat absorbed from the sun
Friction of blood against vessel walls
Digestion of cellulose by gut bacteria
x: Humans are endotherms: their heat is produced inside the body by metabolism, especially respiration in active organs like the liver and muscles.

q: A climber's fingers become pale and cold in freezing wind, while his core temperature stays near 37 °C. This shows that:
o: His hypothalamus has stopped working
His temperature set point has fallen
His fingers produce more heat than his core
Skin arterioles constrict, keeping warm blood in the core at the cost of the extremities
x: Vasoconstriction diverts blood away from the skin, which is why the fingers look pale and cool, but it protects the temperature of the vital organs.

q: On a hot day, a plant can lower the temperature of its leaves mainly by:
o: Closing all its stomata
Growing thicker bark
Transpiration, as evaporation of water from the leaves removes heat
Absorbing more sunlight
x: Evaporation of water during transpiration takes latent heat from the leaf, cooling it. Closing stomata would stop this cooling.

q: Camels in the desert let their body temperature rise by several degrees during the day and lose the stored heat in the cool night. This mainly helps them to:
o: Increase their urine output
Raise their metabolic rate
Save water that would otherwise be lost in sweat
Grow thicker fur
x: By tolerating a higher body temperature by day, the camel needs to sweat far less, conserving scarce water.

q: In the control of body temperature, which pair correctly names the control centre and an effector?
o: Sweat glands and hypothalamus
Skin receptors and kidneys
Thyroid gland and hypothalamus
Hypothalamus and sweat glands
x: The hypothalamus compares body temperature with the set point and sends signals to effectors such as sweat glands, skin arterioles and muscles.

q: On a cold day a person puts on a woollen jacket and drinks hot tea. These are examples of:
o: Responses controlled by thyroxine
Vasodilation of skin arterioles
Behavioural responses to keep warm
Reflex shivering
x: These are actions the person chooses, i.e. behavioural thermoregulation, alongside the automatic physiological responses.

q: If core body temperature fell well below normal, a direct result would be that:
o: Enzymes are denatured immediately
Metabolic rate rises sharply
Sweating increases
Enzyme-controlled reactions slow down, so metabolism slows
x: At low temperature enzymes are not denatured but work slowly, so all metabolic processes, including those of nerves and heart, slow down. This is why constant temperature is needed.

q: The term for animals, such as most bony fishes, whose chief excretory product is ammonia is:
o: Ammonotelic
Ureotelic
Uricotelic
Osmoconformers
x: Ammonotelic animals excrete ammonia, ureotelic animals urea and uricotelic animals uric acid.

q: Spiders excrete much of their nitrogenous waste as:
o: Urea
Ammonia
Guanine
Creatinine
x: Guanine, a purine, is the main nitrogenous waste of spiders. Like uric acid it is insoluble, which saves water on land.

q: Besides ammonia, which nitrogenous compound is excreted by many marine bony fishes?
o: Glycogen
Trimethylamine oxide
Lactic acid
Carbon dioxide
x: Trimethylamine oxide is a nitrogen-containing waste of marine bony fishes. Glycogen, lactic acid and carbon dioxide contain no nitrogen.

q: When an amino acid is deaminated, the part left after removing the amino group can be:
o: Respired for energy or converted to glucose or fat
Excreted directly as urea
Stored unchanged as protein
Converted into haemoglobin
x: Only the nitrogen-containing group becomes ammonia and then urea. The remaining carbon skeleton is used in respiration or stored as glucose or fat.

q: Excess amino acids in the body are deaminated rather than kept because:
o: Amino acids are toxic gases
Amino acids cannot enter the liver
The body cannot store excess amino acids
Amino acids are used only by plants
x: Unlike glucose (stored as glycogen) or fat, surplus amino acids cannot be stored, so their nitrogen is removed and excreted.

q: Ammonia must be removed quickly because even a small build-up in the blood:
o: Causes stones in the kidney
Upsets the pH and harms nerve cells, especially in the brain
Turns blood plasma solid
Increases the oxygen carried by haemoglobin
x: Ammonia is very soluble and alkaline. Small amounts disturb pH and interfere with nerve function, so land animals convert it quickly to less toxic urea.

q: In severe liver failure, which substance rises to dangerous levels in the blood?
o: Urea, because the liver makes too much of it
Uric acid, because the liver breaks down purines faster
Ammonia, because the liver can no longer convert it to urea
Creatinine, because the liver makes it from muscle
x: The ornithine cycle runs in the liver. If the liver fails, ammonia from deamination is not converted to urea and accumulates, poisoning the brain.

q: Insects remove uric acid from their body fluid through:
o: Nephrons
Malpighian tubules
Gills
Contractile vacuoles
x: Malpighian tubules collect wastes from the body fluid and pass uric acid into the gut, where water is reabsorbed and dry waste is passed out.

q: Small aquatic animals such as Hydra can get rid of ammonia simply by:
o: Diffusion across the body surface into the surrounding water
Storing it as crystals inside the body
Converting it to urea in a liver
Filtering it through kidneys
x: Ammonia is very soluble and small molecules diffuse rapidly; in a small water-living animal every cell is close to the water, so no special organ is needed.

q: Mammalian embryos can safely excrete soluble urea, unlike embryos in shelled eggs, because:
o: Mammalian embryos produce no nitrogenous waste
Urea is insoluble and stays in the uterus
The embryo's liver converts urea into uric acid
Urea passes across the placenta into the mother's blood and is removed by her kidneys
x: Inside a sealed egg, waste must be stored, so insoluble uric acid is needed. A mammal's embryo hands its urea to the mother through the placenta.

q: During a dry season in mud, the African lungfish switches from excreting ammonia to making urea. Urea is useful here because it:
o: Is a gas that escapes easily through the skin
Needs more water to excrete than ammonia
Is far less toxic and can be held in the body until water returns
Is completely insoluble and forms crystals
x: Without water to flush ammonia away, the fish makes urea, which is much less toxic and can safely accumulate until it can be excreted.

q: Which of these properties correctly describes urea?
o: It is insoluble and passed as a paste
It is the most toxic nitrogenous waste
It is soluble in water and much less toxic than ammonia
It is made mainly in the kidneys
x: Urea dissolves easily so it is carried in plasma and urine, and it is far less toxic than ammonia. It is made in the liver, not the kidneys.

q: Which statement about uric acid is correct?
o: It is a gas excreted through the lungs
It is more toxic than ammonia
It is only slightly soluble, so it can be passed out with very little water
It is the main waste of bony fishes
x: Uric acid's low solubility lets it be excreted as crystals or paste, saving water. It is the least toxic of the three main wastes.

q: In the ornithine cycle, which compound is regenerated at the end so that the cycle can continue?
o: Ornithine
Citrulline
Arginine
Urea
x: When arginine is split, urea is released and ornithine is reformed, ready to combine with more ammonia and carbon dioxide.

q: In the ornithine cycle, citrulline is converted into arginine by gaining:
o: A molecule of carbon dioxide
A second nitrogen-containing group
A molecule of glucose
A molecule of urea
x: Ornithine first takes up one ammonia (with carbon dioxide) to form citrulline; citrulline then gains a second nitrogen to form arginine. This explains why urea has two nitrogen atoms.

q: The raw materials fed into the ornithine cycle to make urea are:
o: Glucose and oxygen
Uric acid and water
Creatinine and ammonia
Ammonia and carbon dioxide
x: Ammonia from deamination and carbon dioxide from respiration are combined in the liver to form urea, CO(NH2)2.

q: Which nitrogenous waste is produced at a fairly steady daily rate that depends mainly on a person's muscle mass?
o: Creatinine
Uric acid
Ammonia
Urea
x: Creatinine comes from creatine phosphate in muscle, so its output is steady. Urea output varies with protein intake.

q: Which pairing of an animal with its chief excretory product is wrong?
o: Human: urea
Freshwater bony fish: ammonia
Sparrow: urea
Lizard: uric acid
x: Birds such as sparrows excrete uric acid, not urea. The other three pairs are correct.

q: Which pair of animals are both uricotelic?
o: Cow and adult frog
Pigeon and housefly
Goldfish and tadpole
Human and shark
x: Birds and insects excrete uric acid. Cows, adult frogs, humans and sharks are ureotelic; goldfish and tadpoles are ammonotelic.

q: In humans, urea leaves the body mainly in:
o: Faeces
Exhaled air
Tears
Urine
x: Urea is carried in the plasma to the kidneys and excreted in urine. Only small amounts are lost in sweat.

q: Compared with excreting ammonia, excreting urea:
o: Uses more water and needs no energy
Saves water but costs energy to make
Is more toxic to the body
Can only take place through gills
x: Urea is less toxic and can be concentrated, saving water, but making it in the ornithine cycle uses ATP.

q: Some hours after a very protein-rich meal, which change is expected?
o: Glucose appearing in the urine
More urea in the urine
Uric acid crystals in the joints
Ammonia in the exhaled air
x: Surplus amino acids from the meal are deaminated and their nitrogen is turned into urea, so urinary urea rises.
